evidence.text: So I just want to be clear in case there's anything you don't want to share or anything like that. I just want to put that out there. So I'm going to have to be out, but I am a big believer in the category.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Okay. Hi, I'm Debbie. I'm CEO of Copper Cow Coffee, where we reimagine Asian beverages for your home, office, and adventure So my mother is from Vietnam. She emigrated here in ’75 as a refugee. And even though I was born and raised in California, I actually ate Vietnamese food exclusively in my house. I actually remember being in college and bringing all my friends home to my mom's house for brunch and people being totally blown away by all of the flavors, especially Vietnamese coffee. And I thought that people would love Vietnamese coffee if it was just presented to them with really, really great ingredients and innovative packaging that fit their lifestyle

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: But I think that retail success is just the beginning because I think the future of Copper Cow is actually really in selling online as well as into offices. Since launching online earlier this year, we've been growing 20% month over month, completely organically. And then we've also launched an office coffee program this summer, and we're already in over 40 offices. So I'm here today to raise $2 million so that we can have Copper Cow Coffee be a household name.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Great. Tell us a little bit about the product. You said you made it super convenient?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So tell us.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So actually, why don't I make you guys some coffee.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: If you guys are ready for it? Awesome.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: It's very attractive, the packaging.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: Well done.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So the way it comes is a portable pour over so it’s just in this handy little packet You open it up and it just fits over your cup. You tear off the top. And…

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So is pour over, and again, forgive me, because I'm not a coffee drinker, is that unavailable otherwise? Are you the only one doing pour over for in home use?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: There's a couple other companies who are selling a similar format. This format actually comes… If anybody want to try it black first? Okay. Here you go.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: It's a little super strength right now.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: I’ll do it with the condensed... M-hm.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So Vietnamese coffee is kind of known for its strength. The varietal is very caffeinated. This is probably one and a half to two cups of coffee of caffeine.

turns.speaker: Alexandra

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Yeah, this would be awesome for you. Yes

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What is your background?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So my background is, I went to Berkeley and MIT and I used to work at the World Bank in supply chain management and project finance. So the...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: This is your first rodeo in terms of starting a company? First time founder?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Well, actually, I first started about five years ago with a cooking line for you to make Vietnamese food at home. So I did that on the side while I was still at the World Bank. And I got into lots of stores, got into several regions of Whole Foods, Dean and Deluca, a lot of really great stores. But when I would call them and be like, how do I get it to move more? They'd be like, well, it moves great for the category.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: And I began to learn that only 10% of Americans cook. You know, and I need to meet my consumer where they're at. And I'm not going to convince 90% of Americans to cook by an oil and vinegar line. But I, Vietnamese coffee was always top of mind as a product. Because I had so much, I thought, proof of concept of people really loving an elevated Vietnamese food concept.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: And so, and you guys are Vietnamese, so there’s obviously the condensed milk part of it. What percent of your customers are using it just for the coffee versus the Vietnamese coffee? Like the condensed milk add on?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Right. So about 60% of Americans drink their coffee with cream and sugar. And we find about 80% of our customers drink it with the condensed milk.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Okay

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: what's the price point per serving...

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So it really ranges. So in retail it's pretty high. It's about $2 a cup. And that includes, but that includes the creamer

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Okay. So $2 retail. Can you take us through just the numbers quickly? Like what does it cost you? What do you sell it to the retailer for generally speaking?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So we have been selling with a consistent 45% margin for wholesale. Because 80% of our business is still retail because of all the retailers that we're in. Historically it's been a higher margin for ecom, though we're going to kind of reconfigure ecom to be a subscription model where you get months supplies of coffee.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Makes sense. And what are hearing from the retailers? How do they feel about how sales are going for this category? Are they reordering? Are you at that point yet with Walmart?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Yeah. Well, Walmart is selling really well. We're doing about two turns per store per SKU per week. So that's really strong for the price point. And it being a brand new product.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: In the coffee, not the tea?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Both.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: Equally?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: The tea is selling a little bit higher in Walmart.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: Interesting

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Umm

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: do you have a sense within offices who is drinking your coffee repeatedly? right? Is it the junior account executives who are 28? Is it the C suite? Who is it?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So what we find is that people over the age of 35 are not very flexible about trying new coffee drinks. So it’s primarily millennials. Yes. Especially people, the highest conversion is definitely people who have experience with specialty coffee as well as we do have some really diehard umm like fans who know about Vietnamese coffee. But Vietnamese coffee is still a pretty unknown commodity. So...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Yeah, I was going to say like a narrow... I’m not a coffee drinker, but this sounds like a narrow niche that you’re addressing. So how do you get people to try it for the first time if they’re not familiar with Vietnamese coffee?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Well, one thing is definitely just beautiful branding umm I think it’s, even though Vietnamese coffee, if we say just Vietnamese coffee, I think that does sound a little niche. But the idea of it being like a specialty Asian beverage brand It’s definitely, umm I think, something that people want to try.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Do you have a sense in the offices, are people using this as a replacement for K Cup? Or just sort of normal filter coffee? Or is this sort of more like a special treat? How does it play out in the office environment?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So for our smaller office clients, it's a K Cup replacement what some of our other office clients, like Lyft headquarters carries us, they buy about $3000 of Copper Cow a month, and they have 15 types of coffee, and we're just one of the many exotic coffees that they provide.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And so what are you doing in terms of revenue so far?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So last year we did 200,000, and this year we're looking to do 800,000.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Okay

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So Debbie, you're raising $2 million, you said, right?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And what are the terms.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: It's a 5.5 pre money valuation.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And how much of the 2 million has been committed so far?

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I just have to disclose I'm an investor in DripKit.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: I know.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: So I just want to be clear in case there's anything you don't want to share or anything like that. I just want to put that out there. So I'm going to have to be out, but I am a big believer in the category.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: You got a free cup of coffee first, though.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: It's very good. It is very good coffee. And I just wanted to put that out there before she goes into the competition, that's all.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: Very thoughtful of you. Very thoughtful.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Does DripKit, I don’t know about DripKit, do they do pour over coffee?

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: They do. They do. But they don’t do Vietnamese. They do more traditional, it’s more of a traditional single use pour over coffee , I have like three of them in my bag. I travel with them. This is totally a thing. And if you’re a coffee person, this is where coffee is going 100%

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: what’s your differentiation from Dripkit?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Well, first of it’s definitely the blend. Vietnamese coffee has a very different profile than... They’re definitely highlighting a lot of these really light roast single origin coffees, which honestly are a little unforgiving if you mess up the brew. Our Vietnamese coffee, we’re the first people to be introducing third wave Vietnamese coffee. Historically, this is something that’s actually pretty new. Vietnam’s the second largest coffee producer in the world, but just in the past five years have started to have high end beans. So it’s really awesome to introduce that, it’s really smooth, it’s definitely a really, it’s kind of a wonderful foolproof brew.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Can I ask you a slightly different question?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Which is, I feel like I'm a big coffee person. I feel like part of what helped the third wave mainstream coffee people is they were a unit. There were four, five, six roasters who were all pioneering together. And I think if you want to add up Blue Bottle, Intelligentsia, all those folks, they collectively lifted each other's boats.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Totally. I completely agree.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: And is that happening in Vietnamese coffee? Or are you sort of the pioneer?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: No, it's totally happening. In Asia, in general, third wave coffee is really, really exploding Particularly in Vietnam

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: But I mean in the United States, because I feel Blue Bottle, Intelligentsia, Sightglass, those folks, Ritual, they all helped, they didn't collaborate, but because you have four or five really strong brands pioneering high quality coffee, it raised everybody's expectations for what the product should be. And it feels to me like from what you're saying you're on the front wave of the third wave for Vietnamese coffee.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: I would say that I'm the only person who's really bringing high end Vietnamese coffee to the US. Because it’s such a new thing. And it's such a new market and there really isn't an awesome super fun millennial focused accessible coffee company.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So that’s one of my concerns about this. Is that I still view it as being a real niche. And I wonder, when you say it’s on trend, what informs that decision? Why do you think that it’s on trend?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Umm I definitely think it’s the 3000 retailers. How quickly we’ve been able to get into stores. I mean, it’s not, it’s really not common to be in Walmart and your, to be, we got into Walmart 12 months into business.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I agree with you. So what is it about the product that Walmart and these other retailers are attracted to?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: It’s pour over, definitely. And just that high end coffee in retail space is trending. And a lot of really, these great companies that you’re talking about, Blue Bottle, Intelligentsia, La Colombe, you know, they’re really fixated on either a ready to drink beverage, which is heavy and not shippable, or they’re talking about coffee beans. And so this, so both pour over, as well as it being an elevated Asian brand Asian concepts are really, really hitting well with Asian Americans, which is one of the fastest growing consumption areas in the US

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What percentage of your current revenue, let's say for 2018, is from online and what's, what percentage from office and what percentage from retail?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: 80% from retail. 10% from online and 10% from offices.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: What do you want that to be next year?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: I would love it be more of a third, third, third

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What about online? So what's your current customer acquisition cost and what channels are you using?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: That's the thing, is it's been all organic to date. So we haven't really, and that's one of the things that we're really going to figure out with this funding Because when we launched the product line, we did at the fancy food show with a lot of my contacts that I had in the retail space, and we've just been falling ourselves trying to like meet that demand, when really we would like to focus on direct to consumer, on online And so...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How are they finding you currently? When you say it's organic, so how are they...?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: They find it in stores and they buy it online.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I see. Okay. That makes sense.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So who are you going to hire or bring on to help with that since you don’t have a lot of background in online direct marketing.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: So immediately we want to hire a digital growth marketer, someone who can really execute a lot of the Facebook ads, Google ads, things like that. But right now I’m doing lots of ‘dating’ for a more senior head of brand person, or head of ecom. Someone who is experienced building an ecom brand umm Probably from fashion or cosmetics, based in LA

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: Charles, what has been your experience, obviously leaving out any competitive details, in terms of the arc of a brand like this? And what Debbie may run into.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I think the best trend that Debbie has going for her is that I think once you become a pour over person, it’s kind of the only kind of coffee you want to drink.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Why is that?

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: It’s a lifestyle. Like, once you’ve had... I don’t know. I drink a lot of pour over coffee.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Just because it’s easier?

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: No, it’s better. It’s actually not easier. I make pour over at home, I have pearl scale, I’ve got a whole set up. It’s better. It’s cleaner. You get a better, not to get too coffee nerd, you get a better expression of the bean.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Totally.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: It’s just a better coffee experience than French press. And drinking drip brew is yeah. I used to carry a filter and an electric kettle in my suitcase and it was a lot of space.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: Yeah, seriously?

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: No, no, I'm not even kidding you. I used to carry this with me. and like Phil, this will give you a point of reference, a good cup of pour over coffee in New York or San Francisco is going to run you 4 or $5 in a coffee shop.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Or more.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Or more So if you're a pour over person, the idea of being able to have pour over in your office or on the go with you, it's a lifestyle And once you become a pour over person, it's what you want to drink

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: And this is something that takes 60 seconds to make and offers really, really great flavor And so this is what I think is really beautiful about a lot of the great ecom companies that I'm trying to aspire to, is that they really maximize kind of price point as well as luxury. And I feel like Copper Cow does that. We're not the most expensive coffee on the market. We're really, really great coffee that's really easy to make that empowers anybody to make their own coffee without having to think about - do I already own a French press? Do I own a Chemex? Do I own a drip coffee maker?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But how difficult would it be for Starbucks to offer more pour over options? And make it more of a mainstream part of their product mix?

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: I would say that the typical consumer that we're going after, is somebody who wants something better than Starbucks. This is much better than Starbucks coffee. It's much higher grade. You'll be able to taste the difference between a Starbucks or our pour over.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Well, let me get a third party opinion. Charles, you're a coffee snob. You just tasted it.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I avoid Starbucks

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But I want to hear what you think of the quality of...

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I think this is excellent. And I think that this is a very, and I drink, I like Vietnamese coffee, I think this is a very good expression of Vietnamese coffee

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: So on some levels, Debbie, to succeed over some of these other brands, is not just have to get the other small emerging brands, but she has to persuade on some levels Starbucks drinkers to switch.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I disagree. I mean, Blue Bottle was a $700 million outcome with maybe 30 or 40 retail locations at the time that they sold. But a very loyal, high LTV.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: They built a brand. The acquisition was not about how many stores they had. It was about the brand that they built.

turns.speaker: Alexandra
turns.text: Mhmmm

turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: If you’re familiar with coffee company acquisitions, they’re always quite large.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: The multiples are fantastic.

turns.speaker: Debbie

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: There's a lot to like here. You know. Everyone's looking at me. There's a lot to like here. I think... turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Yeah. I guess, you know, I wish... I find myself wishing that you had more traction online.

turns.speaker: Phil

turns.speaker: Phil

turns.text: And I think that’s something that’s come up with investors a lot. And I think that the rebuttal for that is a couple of things. One is that my background, I’m like in analytics all day. turns.speaker: Debbie
turns.text: Great
